title: 2026 U.S. House of Representatives election for Minnesota's 4th Congressional District
description: The 2026 election for Minnesota's 4th Congressional District will be decided in the November 3, 2026 general election, following an August 11, 2026 primary. Incumbent Democrat Betty McCollum, first elected in 2000, is seeking reelection and faces a primary challenge from humanitarian and entrepreneur Aswar Rahman. On the Republican side, multiple candidates including engineer Paul Wikstrom, former law enforcement officer Paul Xiong, and perennial candidate Gene Rechtzigel are competing in the primary. The district, which encompasses Saint Paul and parts of Ramsey and Washington counties, is rated as Safe Democratic by nonpartisan election forecasters.
polling_note: No public opinion polls were found for this race. The district is rated Safe Democratic by major nonpartisan forecasters (Cook Political Report, Inside Elections, Sabato's Crystal Ball), and no competitive polling has been conducted.

candidates.name: Betty McCollum
candidates.summary: Betty McCollum is the incumbent U.S. Representative for Minnesota's 4th Congressional District, first elected in 2000. She previously served in the Minnesota House of Representatives from 1993 to 2001 and is currently the ranking member on the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense. McCollum has been reelected with comfortable margins in the heavily Democratic district and is the dean of Minnesota's congressional delegation.

candidates.name: Aswar Rahman
candidates.summary: Aswar Rahman is a humanitarian, entrepreneur, and filmmaker challenging incumbent Betty McCollum in the Democratic primary. Born in Bangladesh and raised in Minneapolis, Rahman graduated from the University of Minnesota at age 19 and has run businesses in multimedia production and commodities exporting. He previously ran for Mayor of Minneapolis in 2017 and has been active in resettling refugees from Ukraine and Latin America in Minnesota.

candidates.name: Paul Wikstrom
candidates.summary: Paul Wikstrom is an engineer and Republican candidate for Minnesota's 4th Congressional District. He holds a degree in Electrical Engineering from the University of Minnesota and spent over 35 years in engineering and management roles at Minnesota medical device and aerospace companies. Wikstrom previously ran as the Republican nominee for Minnesota House District 40B in 2024 and a 2025 special election, losing both races.

candidates.name: Paul Xiong
candidates.summary: Paul Xiong is a community leader, former law enforcement officer, and Republican candidate for Minnesota's 4th Congressional District. Born in Laos and orphaned at age eight, he came to the United States as an international student and later served as Chairman of the Hmong 18 Council, where he helped raise $3.3 million to establish the Hmong Community Center. Xiong emphasizes public safety, fiscal accountability, and immigration reform as core priorities of his campaign.

candidates.name: Gene Rechtzigel
candidates.summary: Gene Rechtzigel is a Republican candidate for Minnesota's 4th Congressional District who previously ran for the same seat in 2020, receiving 28.97% of the vote against incumbent Betty McCollum. He is running again in the 2026 Republican primary alongside Paul Wikstrom and Paul Xiong.

forecast.rationale: No public polls exist for this race, which limits confidence. However, the district (Saint Paul and parts of Ramsey and Washington counties) is heavily Democratic by partisan baseline and is rated Safe Democratic by all major nonpartisan forecasters (Cook Political Report, Inside Elections, Sabato's Crystal Ball). Incumbent Betty McCollum has held the seat since 2000 and has consistently been reelected with comfortable margins. The Republican primary field includes three candidates; the most recent GOP challenger (Rechtzigel in 2020) received only 28.97%. While McCollum faces a primary challenger (Aswar Rahman), the district's Democratic lean, McCollum's seniority and incumbency, and the lack of any competitive general-election dynamic strongly point to an overwhelming Democratic advantage. The absence of polling prevents high confidence, but the structural fundamentals clearly support a safe Democratic rating.
